paras: The killing of Charles Dew was the murder of a Black farmer in Riley Township, Clinton County, Michigan, who was found beaten and hanged in his barn after the night of August 23, 1881. Weeks or months earlier a party of men had tarred and feathered him and threatened his life, and the killers were never identified in the coverage. Several Eastern papers carried the story under headlines calling it the work of Michigan "Kuklux".

Dew farmed in Riley Township, and was described by one Michigan report as "a small man and not of a fighting disposition" who nevertheless "had many enemies". According to a Detroit dispatch, it was "generally believed in the neighborhood" that he abused his wife and was cruel to his stock, and a party of men broke into his house at night, bound and gagged him, tarred and feathered him, and threatened to kill him if he did not change his course. The papers dated that attack variously to "last spring", about a month before, or about three weeks before the killing.

A Lansing dispatch added that the attackers had been masked and that a few days before his death Dew had gone to St. John's, the county seat, to begin legal proceedings against the men he believed responsible.

On the night of Tuesday, August 23, while his wife was away, Dew's house was "again visited" by persons the Detroit dispatch said were unknown. He was found the next morning hanging from a beam in his barn or granary, with a cut over the left eye that penetrated the skull and another on the back of the head. One leg was dislocated and his back badly bruised, which the Detroit dispatch read as signs of "a terrible struggle". The Lansing dispatch said the gash was "evidently made with an axe", while the Michigan state news said he was struck with "some sharp instrument" and hanged afterward.

Michigan papers reported in early September that there was "no clue" to the murderers, though one said the crime was believed to have been committed by some of his neighbors. In mid-September the Owosso Times reported that the men who had tarred and feathered Dew had been discovered, and that A. W. Burrett had confessed to taking part and implicated seven others. No report of an inquest, an arrest for the killing, or a trial appears in the coverage.

The story reached Eastern papers on August 27 through a Lansing dispatch, which the New-York Tribune ran as "Probable Murder by Hanging" and the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer as "A Persecuted Man". Other papers headed the same text "Kualuxism in Michigan", with the line "Brained With an Ax and Hanged", or "An Outrage by Michigan Kuklux", and it ran as "An Outrage" in Somerset, Pennsylvania. A separate Detroit dispatch, printed in the Alexandria Gazette as "Tar, Feathers and Murder", gave the fullest account of the wounds and of the neighborhood's charges against Dew.

A western crime roundup, "Tragical Tales", reprinted in Wisconsin and Minnesota papers, called Dew "quarrelsome" and stated as fact that he "had abused his wife". In Georgia the Savannah Morning News turned the case against Northern Republicans, remarking that "up in Michigan the lot of a negro farmer is not a happy one" and closing "Call out the troops!" Michigan papers carried the killing in their state-news columns without headlines.

Accounts differ on when Dew was tarred, on whether he died in his granary, barn or house, and on when he was found, the Detroit dispatch giving the morning after Tuesday night and another brief giving Thursday. They also differ on his character: one brief called him quarrelsome, while the Detroit dispatch said he was "not of a quarrelsome disposition" and treated the abuse charges as neighborhood belief.

reader.title: Killing of Charles Dew
bases: Dew, a Black farmer earlier tarred and feathered and threatened with death by a night party of men, was found beaten and hanged in his barn or granary by unknown killers (A1, A2, A11).

Dew was killed and hanged by persons unknown (A2, A11), so the killing was illegal, but no report says how many took part; the earlier tarring was by a 'party of men' who threatened his life over charges that he abused his wife and stock (A2, A11), headlines called it Kuklux work (A5, A6), and a Michigan paper said neighbors were suspected (A14), which points to the same regulating band without any paper saying so.
Independent dispatches from Lansing (A1) and Detroit (A2) and a Michigan state-news item (A11) agree that Dew was found hanged with head wounds in Riley Township after an earlier tarring.

accounts.label: Lansing dispatch (Aug. 26)
accounts.gist: Dew was found dead hanging from a beam in his granary with the left side of his head laid open, months after masked men tarred him and days after he went to the county seat to start legal proceedings against them.

accounts.label: Detroit dispatch (Aug. 27)
accounts.gist: Neighbors who charged him with abusing his wife and stock had tarred him about a month earlier and threatened his life; on Tuesday night his house was visited by unknown persons and he was found next morning hanging in the barn with skull wounds and signs of a struggle.

accounts.label: Michigan state news
accounts.gist: He was killed by blows from a sharp instrument and hanged 'in cold blood'; there was no clue to the killers, though another Michigan paper said neighbors were suspected.

accounts.label: Western news brief
accounts.gist: A negro murdered at his house on the night of the 23d, described as quarrelsome and abusive to his wife, tarred several days earlier by unknown men.

framing.detail: Headlines 'Kualuxism in Michigan' / 'An Outrage by Michigan Kuklux' and 'A Persecuted Man' treated the killing as an outrage by a regulating band.
The New-York Tribune ran it as 'Probable Murder by Hanging' among western news fragments.
The 'Tragical Tales' brief called it murder but described the victim as 'quarrelsome' and abusive to his wife.
The Savannah Morning News used the case sarcastically against the 'Republican North' ('Call out the troops!') without condemning the killing itself.

conflicts.note: The Detroit dispatch and the Michigan state-news item agree on a recent tarring; the Lansing dispatch says last spring.
A granary may be part of the barn; the 'at his house' brief is a condensed summary.
The Detroit dispatch is the most specific.

His farm in Riley Township; found in his granary (A1, A4) or barn (A2, A11, A14); one brief says murdered 'at his house' (A8).
Charles Dew (also printed Chas. Dew, Charley Dew, Chester Dew, Charles Dow, Dow), a 'colored farmer' or 'negro'.
No accusation is tied to the killing. The earlier tarring followed neighborhood charges that he abused his wife and was cruel to his stock.

Unknown: 'by whom is not known' (A2), 'no clue to his murderers' (A11); a Michigan paper said the crime was believed committed 'by some of his neighbors' (A14). The tarring was by masked men (A1) or 'a party of men' (A2).
